1254.title: God our mother
1254.hook: Julian of Norwich wrote of Jesus as our true mother
1254.howItsDone: Some Christians pray with Julian of Norwich's words and read her Revelations of Divine Love; churches keep the Father language of the creeds and the Lord's Prayer, and some also use scripture's mother images for God's care, as in Isaiah 66:13.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ockham's razor: don't multiply things without need. Your line was keep it simple.

A woman lies so sick that the people around her expect her to die. A priest holds a crucifix before her face. Then, as she later wrote, she was given a series of showings: visions of Christ and his love. She recovered, kept thinking about what she had seen, and wrote it down. You met her in years one and three: Julian of Norwich, a woman who lived a life of prayer beside a church in that English city. Among the things she wrote is this: Jesus is our mother.

Julian wasn't throwing out the old words. She calls God our Father, plainly and often. But she sets the two side by side: as truly as God is our Father, God is our Mother. And she gives the motherhood above all to Jesus. Why Jesus? Look at what a mother does. She carries a child in her own body and brings it into life through pain; Julian looks at the cross and sees Christ laboring to bring us to birth. A mother feeds her child from herself; Julian sees Christ feeding his people with himself in the sacrament. A mother doesn't stop loving a child who falls in the mud; she picks it up and washes it. Julian says Christ does the same when we fail, without contempt. She didn't invent the picture out of nothing. Scripture already holds it. In Isaiah, God says, "As one whom his mother comforteth, so will I comfort you." And earlier: "Can a woman forget her sucking child, that she should not have compassion on the son of her womb? yea, they may forget, yet will I not forget thee." Jesus himself, grieving over Jerusalem, says, "how often would I have gathered thy children together, even as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings." Julian wove a picture like this into a whole way of seeing. Christians use her picture in different ways. Some pray with her words. Others keep to the Father language of the creeds and the Lord's Prayer while still honoring her. Julian herself held both, and saw no contest between them.

Bring to mind one picture of that kind of care: a cool hand on a feverish forehead, a child lifted up after a fall, someone awake in the night with a crying baby. If your own story with a mother is hard, choose a different picture; anyone who has cared like that will do. Let it stay a while, and if you pray, hold it up to God the way Julian did.
God our mother. Julian of Norwich's picture of Christ who births, feeds and lifts us up, as truly as God is our Father.
Your line: our true mother. Care that picks you up without contempt. I'll be here tomorrow.

1255.title: The freedom of a Christian
1255.hook: Luther: a Christian is free lord of all, and dutiful servant of all
1255.howItsDone: Lutheran and other Protestant Christians read Luther's treatise as a classic statement of faith and freedom; across churches, Christians practice service to neighbors through charity, volunteering, and ordinary acts of care.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Julian of Norwich and God our mother. Your line was our true mother.

Two sentences, side by side, that seem to cancel each other out. A Christian is a free lord of all, subject to no one. A Christian is a dutiful servant of all, subject to everyone. Martin Luther, whose hammer you met in year one, set those two at the top of a short book called The Freedom of a Christian, and spent the rest of it showing why both are true at once. Free and bound. Lord and servant. It sounds like a riddle.

Luther's freedom starts somewhere unexpected: not with what a person does, but with what a person receives. For Luther, someone is made right with God by faith, by trusting God's promise in Christ, not by piling up good works. That's the lord-of-all half. In Luther's telling, nothing a person fails at can take away what God has given, and nobody is working to earn their place. So the Christian is free. Then comes the turn. Free for what? Luther's answer: for the neighbor. Because Christians don't need good works to save themselves, they can give those works away. Works stop being a ladder you climb and become a gift you hand across the fence. He took the pattern from Paul: "For though I be free from all men, yet have I made myself servant unto all." And again: "Owe no man any thing, but to love one another." To the Galatians, Paul puts both halves in one breath: "ye have been called unto liberty; only use not liberty for an occasion to the flesh, but by love serve one another." Luther even pictures a Christian becoming a kind of Christ to the neighbor, giving freely as Christ gave. Christians describe faith and works in different ways. Lutheran churches follow Luther closely here. Catholic and Orthodox Christians also teach that grace comes first and that love must act, while explaining how faith and works fit together in their own terms. In each of them, the neighbor still gets served.

Bring to mind one small service for someone who can't pay you back and might not even notice: a neighbor's bin, a coworker's extra task, the dish someone left in the sink. Watch where your mind goes, will they thank me, will it count, and let those questions drop, picturing it done out of freedom, with nothing to earn. If you pray, you can offer it to God.
The freedom of a Christian. Luther's two sentences: free lord of all, through faith; dutiful servant of all, through love.

1256.title: The theology of the cross
1256.hook: Luther: God is found in weakness and suffering, not in glory
1256.howItsDone: Lutheran Christians, and others who draw on Luther, speak of the theology of the cross in preaching and pastoral care; across churches, Christians keep the crucifix or cross in view and visit the sick and dying as places where Christ is met.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Luther's two sentences: free lord of all, servant of all. Your line was free and a servant.

Where would someone go looking for God? A mountain at sunrise, maybe. A cathedral full of music. A winning streak that seems to say, someone up there is on my side. Martin Luther gave a sharp answer, and it wasn't any of those. The place to look, he said, is a man dying on a cross: mocked, abandoned and weak. Speaking at a gathering of his own religious order, he drew a line between two kinds of theologian: a theologian of glory, and a theologian of the cross.

A theologian of glory, Luther said, tries to read God off the world's strength: power, success, splendor, whatever impresses. It sounds reasonable. But it ends up calling evil good and good evil, because it can't see God anywhere that looks like failure. A theologian of the cross calls a thing what it actually is. He looks at Good Friday and says: there. God is there, hidden in suffering and weakness. Luther took his lead from Paul: "Because the foolishness of God is wiser than men; and the weakness of God is stronger than men." Paul had begged to be rid of something he called a thorn in the flesh, and the answer he heard was: "My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness." In the disputation itself, Luther also points to a line from Isaiah: "Verily thou art a God that hidest thyself." So in Luther's picture, God isn't missing from the hard places. God is hidden in them, on purpose, where people don't think to look. Then a hospital room looks different. So does a business that failed, or a body that won't heal. A theologian of glory asks, what did I do wrong to end up here? A theologian of the cross asks, is God here too? Luther doesn't call suffering good in itself. He says God meets people inside it. Christians who keep a crucifix in sight, or who sit up with the dying, are saying something close to this without a word of theology.

Bring to mind one weak place, a fear or failure of your own, or a friend who is sick or struggling, and look at it honestly without rushing to fix it. Then ask quietly: could God be here too? If you pray, ask it of God directly. If the weight ever feels too heavy, or you're thinking of harming yourself, call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.
The theology of the cross. Luther's teaching that God is found hidden in weakness and suffering, above all at the cross, not read off the world's glory.

1257.title: Providence
1257.hook: Calvin: nothing happens by chance; God holds all things
1257.howItsDone: Christians speak of God's providence in prayer and in hard times, often with Joseph's words from Genesis 50:20; Reformed churches teach it in Calvin's strong form, and other churches confess it while describing human freedom in their own ways.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Luther's theology of the cross: God hidden where people don't think to look. Your line was God hidden in weakness.

Joseph's brothers stand in front of him in Egypt, terrified. Long ago they threw him into a pit and sold him. Now he's the man who decides whether their families eat. Their father has just died, and they're sure revenge is coming. Joseph weeps. Then he tells them: "ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good." You heard that line back in year two. One event, two intentions inside it. John Calvin built a whole teaching on lines like that, under the name providence.

Calvin taught that nothing happens by chance. The world isn't a machine God wound up and walked away from, and it isn't a dice game either. God holds all things and steers them. He leaned on Jesus's words about sparrows sold in the market: "Are not two sparrows sold for a farthing? and one of them shall not fall on the ground without your Father. But the very hairs of your head are all numbered." And on a proverb: "The lot is cast into the lap; but the whole disposing thereof is of the LORD." Even a cast lot doesn't fall outside God's hand. For Calvin this wasn't a cold idea to argue about. He wrote that knowing God's providence brings thankfulness when things go well, patience when they don't, and freedom from anxiety about what's coming. If the future is in God's hand, he reasoned, a believer doesn't have to hold all of it alone. Christians understand providence in different ways. Reformed churches follow Calvin closely, with strong words about God's governing of every event. Catholic, Orthodox, Methodist and other Christians also confess God's providence, while describing human freedom and chance in their own ways. And they read the same Joseph. Notice when he says his line: not from the bottom of the pit, but years later, looking back over the whole road. Providence in Genesis is something Joseph sees in the rearview mirror. While it was happening, it only looked like a pit.

Bring to mind one thing you can't control, a test result, a decision someone else will make, a child far away, and notice how your hands want to grip it. Let them open on your lap. If you pray, hand that one thing to God, held in a hand bigger than yours; if you don't, notice what it's like to set it down for these two minutes.
Providence. Calvin's teaching that God holds and steers all things, so that nothing happens by chance.
Your line: held in his hand. Joseph saw it looking back. That's today, done.

1258.title: Richard Hooker
1258.hook: an Anglican theologian of patient reason and tradition
1258.howItsDone: Anglican and Episcopal Christians look to Richard Hooker when they speak of scripture, reason and tradition together; churches across traditions weigh these three in different ways in their teaching and decisions.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Calvin and providence: nothing by chance, seen looking back. Your line was held in his hand.

One London church, two preachers who disagreed. The story is often told that one of them preached in the morning and the other answered him from the same pulpit in the afternoon, Sunday after Sunday. The congregation got a debate with their sermons. One of those preachers was Richard Hooker. Years later, away from London, he wrote a long, careful book on the questions behind that quarrel, Of the Laws of Ecclesiastical Polity. He was an Anglican theologian who argued without contempt.

Hooker's opponents held that the church's order and worship should be drawn from scripture, chapter and verse. Hooker gave scripture first place too. But he asked a quiet question: is scripture the only light God gives? His answer was no. God is a God of order, Hooker said, and gave human beings reason, the power to see what is good and fitting, as a gift. Where scripture speaks plainly, it rules. Where it's silent, Christians use reason, and they listen to what the church has learned over the centuries, its tradition. Later teachers summed this up in a picture, a three-legged stool: scripture, reason, tradition. The stool isn't in Hooker's book, and he gave scripture more weight than an even stool suggests. But the picture catches one thing he cared about: no single support has to carry everything alone. For Hooker, reason wasn't faith's enemy; scripture invites it. In Isaiah the LORD says, "Come now, and let us reason together." And First Peter asks Christians to be ready "to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear." With meekness. Hooker's style matched those words. He wrote about the people he disagreed with without sneering, and tried to state their case fairly before he answered it. Anglican churches look back to him as one of their shaping voices. Other Christians weigh scripture, reason and tradition differently, and argue about how. Hooker's way suggests the argument itself can be held with patience.

Bring to mind someone you disagree with, about church, politics, family plans, anything, and try Hooker's habit: state their view in your head as fairly as you can, the way they'd put it on a good day, until they might nod along. Notice the urge to slip in a jab, and leave it out. If you pray, you can pray for that person by name.
Richard Hooker. The Anglican theologian of patient reason: scripture first, with reason and tradition as gifts beside it.
Your line: reason is a gift. Hooker held it beside scripture, with patience. Until tomorrow.

1259.title: Reasons of the heart
1259.hook: Pascal: the heart has its reasons, which reason does not know
1259.howItsDone: Christians read Pascal's Pensées as a classic of faith and reason; across churches, Christians speak of knowing God with the heart as well as the mind, in prayer, worship, and quiet reflection.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Richard Hooker and patient reason. Your line was reason is a gift.

After Blaise Pascal died, the story goes, a servant found a folded paper sewn into the lining of his coat. On it Pascal had written about one night when, as he tells it, he met God. You met that night of fire in year three. Near the top, after the date, stands a single word: fire. It names the God of Abraham, of Isaac, of Jacob, and adds: not of the philosophers and the scholars. Pascal was a mathematician, a man of proofs. And a note with no proof in it was the one he kept in his coat.

Pascal left behind a pile of notes for a book he never finished. They were gathered after his death as the Pensées, his thoughts. In one of them he writes: "The heart has its reasons, which reason does not know." The line often gets used to mean, feelings beat facts. Pascal meant something sharper. He trusted reason; he did mathematics. But he noticed that some things we know without proving them: that we're awake and not dreaming, the first principles that all our proofs start from. These, he said, we know by the heart, a kind of direct knowing underneath argument. And faith, for Pascal, lives there too. In another note he says it is the heart, not the reason, that perceives God. That isn't giving up on thinking. It's honesty about where thinking starts. Scripture gives the heart that kind of weight. Proverbs says, "Keep thy heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life." And when the shepherds have told what they saw at the manger, Luke says, "But Mary kept all these things, and pondered them in her heart." Pondering in the heart: not feeling instead of thinking, but thinking all the way down. Pascal's night of fire wasn't the end of an argument. It was more like recognizing a voice in a crowded room before you can explain how you know it. And still he went on writing arguments, because for him the head and the heart were meant to work together.

Bring to mind something you know but can't fully prove: that a certain person loves you, that a choice you made was right, that a place is home. Don't argue for it; let it be known, the way Pascal said the heart knows, and notice whether it holds steady when you stop defending it. If you pray, you can bring that knowing to God and rest in it.
Reasons of the heart. Pascal's line: the heart knows some things, God among them, that reason can't reach by proof alone.
Your line: the heart has reasons. Pascal kept his in a coat lining. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1260.title: Edwards on beauty
1260.hook: Jonathan Edwards saw God as the source of all beauty
1260.howItsDone: Christians who read Jonathan Edwards, especially in Reformed and evangelical churches, speak of God's beauty and glory; across churches, Christians pray the Psalms of creation and worship "in the beauty of holiness" through music, art and attention to the natural world.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pascal and the reasons of the heart. Your line was the heart has reasons.

A young man walks alone in his father's pasture, looking up at the sky and the clouds. Later he wrote that something had changed in how he saw everything. God's glory seemed to show in the sun and moon and stars, in the clouds, the grass, the flowers, even in thunder, which used to frighten him. His name was Jonathan Edwards, a New England preacher.

For Edwards, beauty isn't decoration added on top of religion. It sits close to the center. God, he taught, is beautiful in himself, and every lovely thing in the world is a kind of echo or shadow of that beauty. A sunset is borrowed light. When Edwards tried to say what real goodness is, he talked about harmony: beings in loving agreement with one another, the way notes agree in a chord. Holiness, in his eyes, wasn't grim. It was lovely. He found that in the Bible. Psalm 19: "The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament sheweth his handywork." Psalm 96: "O worship the LORD in the beauty of holiness." And the one request in Psalm 27, a psalm of David: "One thing have I desired of the LORD, that will I seek after; that I may dwell in the house of the LORD all the days of my life, to behold the beauty of the LORD." To behold. Not to argue about, not to prove. To look. Edwards could preach fiercely about judgment, and the same man wrote about God's glory in snow and sky and a field of flowers. Both were real to him. For Edwards, the change he called conversion was something like gaining a new sense, a taste for that beauty. He compared it to honey: you can hear honey described all day, but you only know its sweetness by tasting it. That closes a week of thinkers: Julian's mother love, Luther's freedom and his cross, Calvin's providence, Hooker's reason, Pascal's heart, and Edwards's beauty.

segments.voice: Let your eyes find one beautiful thing nearby, or one you can call up from memory: light on a wall, a tree outside the window, a face you love, the sound of rain. Behold it, the psalm's word, and stay with it longer than feels normal, coming back whenever your mind wanders. If you pray, you can let it lead you toward the one Edwards believed it echoes.
Edwards on beauty. Jonathan Edwards's teaching that God is beautiful, and that every beauty in the world reflects that beauty.
